claim: Head-fixed behavioral experiments in rodents permit unparalleled experimental control, precise measurement of behavior, and concurrent modulation and measurement of neural activity.
source: Head-fixed behavioral experiments in rodents permit unparalleled experimental control, precise measurement of behavior, and concurrent modulation and measurement of neural activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about the advantages of head-fixed experiments, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claim: Head-fixed mice tested with OHRBETS displayed operant conditioning for caloric reward that replicates core behavioral phenotypes observed during freely moving conditions.
source: Head-fixed mice tested with OHRBETS displayed operant conditioning for caloric reward that replicates core behavioral phenotypes observed during freely moving conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing head-fixed and freely moving conditions.

claim: OHRBETS permits optogenetic intracranial self-stimulation under positive or negative operant conditioning procedures.
source: OHRBETS also permits optogenetic intracranial self-stimulation under positive or negative operant conditioning procedures and real-time place preference behavior, like that observed in freely moving assays.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data showing optogenetic reinforcement in the manuscript.

claim: OHRBETS permits real-time place preference behavior like that observed in freely moving assays.
source: OHRBETS also permits optogenetic intracranial self-stimulation under positive or negative operant conditioning procedures and real-time place preference behavior, like that observed in freely moving assays.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing wheel time preference to freely moving real-time place testing.

claim: In a multi-spout brief-access consumption task, mice displayed licking as a function of concentration of sucrose, quinine, and sodium chloride.
source: In a multi-spout brief-access consumption task, mice displayed licking as a function of concentration of sucrose, quinine, and sodium chloride, with licking modulated by homeostatic or circadian influences.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data showing concentration-dependent licking behavior.

claim: Licking in the multi-spout task was modulated by homeostatic or circadian influences.
source: In a multi-spout brief-access consumption task, mice displayed licking as a function of concentration of sucrose, quinine, and sodium chloride, with licking modulated by homeostatic or circadian influences.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differences in licking behavior under different homeostatic states and light/dark cycles.

claim: Mesolimbic dopamine signals during the multi-spout brief-access task display strong correlations with relative solution value and magnitude of consumption.
source: Finally, to highlight the functionality of OHRBETS, we measured mesolimbic dopamine signals during the multi-spout brief-access task that display strong correlations with relative solution value and magnitude of consumption.
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data showing correlations between GRAB-DA signals and licking behavior.

claim: Head fixation offers high degrees of behavioral control that enables consistent delivery of stimuli to the animal.
source: At the cost of reduced naturalistic behavior and enhanced stress, head fixation offers high degrees of behavioral control that enables consistent delivery of stimuli to the animal, precise measurement of behavior, and isolation of subcomponents of behavior (Bjerre and Palmer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Head fixation comes at the cost of reduced naturalistic behavior and enhanced stress.
source: At the cost of reduced naturalistic behavior and enhanced stress, head fixation offers high degrees of behavioral control that enables consistent delivery of stimuli to the animal, precise measurement of behavior, and isolation of subcomponents of behavior (Bjerre and Palmer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge about limitations of head-fixed approaches.

claim: Head fixation enables precise measurement of behavior and isolation of subcomponents of behavior.
source: At the cost of reduced naturalistic behavior and enhanced stress, head fixation offers high degrees of behavioral control that enables consistent delivery of stimuli to the animal, precise measurement of behavior, and isolation of subcomponents of behavior (Bjerre and Palmer, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Head-fixed behavioral approaches offer enhanced compatibility with neuroscience approaches that require tethers including optogenetics and fiber photometry.
source: By removing turning associated with locomotion, head-fixed behavioral approaches offer enhanced compatibility with neuroscience approaches that require tethers including optogenetics and fiber photometry.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the advantages of head fixation for tethered approaches.

claim: Head fixation is compatible with tools for measuring and manipulating neuronal activity at the single cell level, including two-photon calcium imaging and holographic optogenetics.
source: Furthermore, head fixation is also compatible with tools for measuring and manipulating neuronal activity at the single cell level, including two-photon calcium imaging and holographic optogenetics.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the compatibility of head fixation with advanced imaging techniques.

claim: Motivated behaviors are essential for survival and can be disrupted in brain circuits, leading to various diseases such as addiction and obesity.
source: Motivated behaviors are essential for survival and can be disrupted in brain circuits, leading to various diseases such as addiction and obesity (Kenny, 2011; Rossi and Stuber, 2018; Volkow et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Motivation in animal models is often assessed using multiple tasks that attempt to isolate distinct behavioral components such as appetitive and consummatory behaviors.
source: Motivation in animal models is often assessed and quantified using multiple tasks that attempt to isolate distinct behavioral components such as appetitive and consummatory behaviors that can be the product of independent or overlapping brain circuits (Panksepp, 1982; Robinson and Berridge, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established knowledge about behavioral assessment methods.

claim: Appetitive and consummatory behaviors can be the product of independent or overlapping brain circuits.
source: Motivation in animal models is often assessed and quantified using multiple tasks that attempt to isolate distinct behavioral components such as appetitive and consummatory behaviors that can be the product of independent or overlapping brain circuits (Panksepp, 1982; Robinson and Berridge, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The brief-access task consists of trial-based presentations of one of multiple solutions, enabling recording of behavioral and neuronal responses to gradations of both rewarding and aversive solutions within a single session.
source: A particularly useful model is the brief-access task, which consists of trial-based presentations of one of multiple solutions, enabling recording of behavioral and neuronal responses to gradations of both rewarding and aversive solutions within a single session (Boughter et al., 2002; Davis, 1973; Smith, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations describing the brief-access task methodology.

claim: There has been limited adaptation of freely moving behavioral tasks for head-fixed rodents despite the advantages afforded by the head-fixed approach.
source: Despite the widespread use of these procedures in freely moving animals, there has been limited adaptation of these tasks for head-fixed rodents despite the advantages afforded by the of the head-fixed approach.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: OHRBETS is a low-cost, open-source platform of hardware and software for quantifying both operant and consummatory behavior in head-fixed mice.
source: Here, we present OHRBETS (Open-Source Head-fixed Rodent Behavioral Experimental Training System), a low-cost, open-source platform of hardware and software for quantifying both operant and consummatory behavior in head-fixed mice.
evidence: This is a direct description of the system presented in the manuscript.

claim: OHRBETS features the ability to precisely limit operant and consummatory behaviors during operant conditioning, replicating the retractable levers and spout aspects of the freely moving condition.
source: OHRBETS features the ability to precisely limit operant and consummatory behaviors during operant conditioning, replicating the retractable levers and spout aspects of the freely moving condition.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the functionality of the retractable spout and wheel brake.

claim: OHRBETS has a multi-spout design that allows multiple solutions to be presented independently in a single behavioral session.
source: OHRBETS has a multi-spout design that allows multiple solutions to be presented independently in a single behavioral session, enabling various behavioral experiments like probabilistic reinforcement tasks and choice behavior.
evidence: This is supported by the description and experimental data from the multi-spout experiments.

claim: The total cost per OHRBETS system is around $600 for the operant-only version and around $1000 for the operant+multi-spout version.
source: Our system consists of custom 3D printed and inexpensive, commercially available components bringing the total cost to around $600 for the operant-only version and around $1000 for the operant+multi-spout version.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the cost of the system based on the components used.

claim: The retractable spout follows a consistent and reliable pattern with >98% of extensions reaching a terminal position within 0.3 mm of each other in under 180 ms of the extension command.
source: We found that the retractable spout follows a consistent and reliable pattern with >98% of extensions reaching a terminal position within 0.3 mm of each other in under 180 ms of the extension command (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from high-speed video recording and DeepLabCut analysis.

claim: The wheel brake rapidly stopped wheel rotation in 100% of trials, even with manual velocities that exceed that which a mouse can produce.
source: The wheel brake rapidly stopped wheel rotation in 100% of trials, even with manual velocities that exceed that which a mouse can produce (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data testing the wheel brake functionality.

claim: Most mouse-generated rotations ceased in under 250 ms after brake engagement.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the effectiveness of the brake to stop wheel rotation in data obtained during operant conditioning experiments and found that most mouse-generated rotations ceased in under 250 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–I).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of behavioral data during operant conditioning.

claim: By the third session of retractable spout training, 31 out of 31 mice licked during 90% of trials.
source: By the third session of training, 31 out of 31 mice licked during 90% of trials (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data from the training sessions.

claim: Mice demonstrated a learned association between spout extension and a simultaneous auditory tone with the availability of sucrose, as they reduced their latency from spout extension to first lick across the three sessions of training.
source: Mice demonstrated a learned association between spout extension and a simultaneous auditory tone with the availability of sucrose, as they reduced their latency from spout extension to first lick across the three sessions of training (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing reduced latency over training sessions.

claim: Mice learned to turn the wheel to obtain 10% sucrose in as little as one session, as 25/31 mice showed greater rotation in the active direction compared to the inactive direction.
source: We found that mice learned to turn the wheel to obtain 10% sucrose in as little as one session, as 25/31 mice showed greater rotation in the active direction compared to the inactive direction (Figure 2G, session 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data from the first operant conditioning session.

claim: By the sixth session of operant conditioning, 29/31 mice showed net rotation in the active direction.
source: By the sixth session of operant conditioning, 29/31 mice showed net rotation in the active direction (Figure 2G, data from all sessions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), that was the product of increased rotation in the active direction and no change in rotation in the inactive direction (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is directly supported by behavioral data from the sixth operant conditioning session.

claim: As a group, mice showed significantly more rotation in the active direction compared to the inactive direction starting at the second session.
source: As a group, mice showed significantly more rotation in the active direction compared to the inactive direction starting at the second session (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data across training sessions.

claim: Female mice exhibit a reduced total active rotation over the course of training sessions.
source: Notably, we found that over the course of training sessions, female mice exhibit a reduced total active rotation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3H), reduced total lick count (Figure 2—figure supplement 3Q), and reduced bias for rotation in the active direction (Figure 2—figure supplement 3T).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing male and female mice.

claim: When the cost of reward was increased, mice significantly increased responding in the active direction but not the inactive direction.
source: As observed in freely moving rodents (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), when we increased the cost of reward, mice significantly increased responding in the active direction but not the inactive direction (Figure 2J, all sessions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A), indicating that they show flexible response rates as a function of reward cost (Kliner et al., 1988; Winger and Woods, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing different fixed ratio costs and citations to prior work.

claim: Under both progressive ratio schedules, mice responded for rewards and displayed increased breakpoints for greater reward magnitude.
source: Under both schedules, mice responded for rewards during progressive ratio and displayed increased breakpoints for greater reward magnitude (Reilly, 1999; Sclafani and Ackroff, 2003; Winger and Woods, 1985; Figure 2K, right).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from progressive ratio sessions and citations to prior work.

claim: Mice displayed reversal learning, as they reversed the terminal cumulative position following contingency reversal and training over seven sessions.
source: We found that mice displayed reversal learning, as they reversed the terminal cumulative position (initially active-initially inactive) following contingency reversal and training over seven sessions (Heyser et al., 2000; Klanker et al., 2015; Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from reversal training and citations to prior work.

claim: Mice showed similar changes in response vigor with increased cost of reward in head-fixed and freely moving versions of operant conditioning.
source: We found that mice showed similar changes in response vigor with increased cost of reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) and similar pattern of reduction in responding over the course of a session after the first 10 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but earned more liquid in the freely moving version of the task (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral data from head-fixed and freely moving conditions.

claim: Mice earned more liquid in the freely moving version of the operant task compared to the head-fixed version.
source: We found that mice showed similar changes in response vigor with increased cost of reward (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C) and similar pattern of reduction in responding over the course of a session after the first 10 min (Figure 2—figure supplement 4D) but earned more liquid in the freely moving version of the task (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of weight gain data from head-fixed and freely moving conditions.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of lateral hypothalamic area GABAergic neurons produces positive reinforcement.
source: We used optogenetic stimulation of lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) GABAergic neurons (LHAGABA) as a appetitive unconditioned stimulus because activation of these neurons produces positive reinforcement (Jennings et al., 2015), and optogenetic stimulation of LHA glutamatergic neurons (LHAGlut) as an aversive unconditioned stimulus because activation of these neurons is aversive (Chen et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing these effects.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of LHA glutamatergic neurons is aversive.
source: We used optogenetic stimulation of lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) GABAergic neurons (LHAGABA) as a appetitive unconditioned stimulus because activation of these neurons produces positive reinforcement (Jennings et al., 2015), and optogenetic stimulation of LHA glutamatergic neurons (LHAGlut) as an aversive unconditioned stimulus because activation of these neurons is aversive (Chen et al., 2020; Rossi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work establishing these effects.

claim: LHAGABA:ChR2 mice displayed high levels of operant responding for the active hole or active direction and displayed strong discrimination between active and inactive responses.
source: On the last 20 Hz self-stimulation training session, Vgat-Cre mice expressing ChR2 in the LHA (LHAGABA:ChR2) displayed high levels of operant responding for the active hole or active direction and displayed strong discrimination between active and inactive responses; Vgat-Cre mice expressing the mCherry control construct in the LHA (LHAGABA:Control) displayed little to no responding and did not discriminate between responses (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic reinforcement experiments.

claim: LHAGABA:Control mice displayed little to no responding and did not discriminate between responses during optogenetic reinforcement.
source: On the last 20 Hz self-stimulation training session, Vgat-Cre mice expressing ChR2 in the LHA (LHAGABA:ChR2) displayed high levels of operant responding for the active hole or active direction and displayed strong discrimination between active and inactive responses; Vgat-Cre mice expressing the mCherry control construct in the LHA (LHAGABA:Control) displayed little to no responding and did not discriminate between responses (Figure 3D and F).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from control mice in optogenetic reinforcement experiments.

claim: In both the freely moving and head-fixed conditions, LHAGABA:ChR2 mice displayed greater active response rates for higher stimulation frequencies.
source: In both the freely moving and head-fixed conditions, LHAGABA:ChR2 mice displayed greater active response rates for higher stimulation frequencies (Figure 3E, G and H) that were positively correlated across the two versions of the task (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data across different stimulation frequencies in both conditions.

claim: Active response rates for optogenetic stimulation were positively correlated across freely moving and head-fixed versions of the task in LHAGABA:ChR2 mice.
source: In both the freely moving and head-fixed conditions, LHAGABA:ChR2 mice displayed greater active response rates for higher stimulation frequencies (Figure 3E, G and H) that were positively correlated across the two versions of the task (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data across conditions.

claim: Mice rapidly ceased responding once optogenetic stimulation was withheld and resumed responding once optogenetic stimulation was reintroduced.
source: Similar to freely moving positive optogenetic reinforcement (Stuber et al., 2011; Witten et al., 2011), mice rapidly ceased responding once optogenetic stimulation was withheld and resumed responding once optogenetic stimulation was reintroduced (Figure 3—figure supplement 4, left).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data during extinction and reinstatement and citations to prior work.

claim: LHAGlut:ChR2 mice displayed high levels of responding in the active direction and strong discrimination between the active and inactive directions under negative reinforcement.
source: Following training, Vglut2-Cre mice with expression of ChR2 in the LHA (LHAGlut:ChR2) displayed high levels of responding in the active direction and strong discrimination between the active and inactive directions, while Vglut2-Cre mice with expression of mCherry control construct in the LHA (LHAGlut:Control) displayed little to no responding and no discrimination (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from negative reinforcement experiments.

claim: LHAGlut:ChR2 mice acquired negative reinforcement behavior at a reduced rate compared to positive reinforcement for LHAGABA optogenetic stimulation.
source: LHAGlut:ChR2 mice acquired negative reinforcement behavior at a reduced rate compared to positive reinforcement for LHAGABA optogenetic stimulation (seven sessions to acquisition of negative reinforcement vs one session for positive reinforcement; Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, K).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of training data across different reinforcement procedures.

claim: Compared to LHAGlut:Control mice, LHAGlut:ChR2 mice displayed suppressed amounts of active-responding, number of pauses earned, and inactive responding during the freely moving negative reinforcement condition.
source: We found that, compared to LHAGlut:Control mice, LHAGlut:ChR2 mice displayed suppressed amounts of active-responding, number of pauses earned, and inactive responding during the freely moving condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G–I).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from freely moving negative reinforcement experiments.

claim: The discrepancy between acquisition of negative reinforcement in the head-fixed assay versus the freely moving assay could be attributed to the reduced range of actions mice can make in the head-fixed assay.
source: The discrepancy between acquisition of negative reinforcement in the head-fixed assay versus the freely moving assay could be attributed to the reduced range of actions mice can make in the head-fixed assay.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences in behavior between conditions.

claim: Mice expressing mCherry did not show preference nor aversion for the stimulation paired chamber/zone across all stimulation frequencies in both the freely moving and head-fixed procedures.
source: Specifically, mice expressing mCherry (LHA:Control mice) did not show preference nor aversion for the stimulation paired chamber/zone across all stimulation frequencies in both the freely moving and head-fixed procedures (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from control mice in RTPT/WTP experiments.

claim: LHAGABA:ChR2 mice showed strong place preference while LHAGlut:ChR2 mice showed strong place aversion for the paired chamber/zone with higher stimulation frequencies compared to lower stimulation frequencies.
source: On the contrary, LHAGABA:ChR2 mice showed strong place preference while LHAGlut:ChR2 mice showed strong place aversion for the paired chamber/zone with higher stimulation frequencies compared to lower stimulation frequencies (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from RTPT/WTP experiments.

claim: There was no statistical difference between the amount of time in the paired chamber/zone in the freely moving and head-fixed versions of the RTPT/WTP task.
source: There was no statistical difference between the amount of time in the paired chamber/zone in the freely moving and head-fixed versions of the task (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing the two versions of the task.

claim: The time in the paired chamber/zone was correlated across freely moving RTPT and head-fixed WTP for LHAGABA:ChR2 and LHAGlut:ChR2 mice, but not LHA:Control mice.
source: Furthermore, the time in the paired chamber/zone was correlated across freely moving RTPT and head-fixed WTP for LHAGABA:ChR2 and LHAGlut:ChR2 mice, but not LHA:Control mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of behavioral data across conditions.

claim: The total number of licks during each session is strongly correlated with weight in fluid consumed during the session.
source: The licks measured using this approach approximate consumption, as total number of licks during each session is strongly correlated with weight in fluid consumed during the session (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of lick count and weight gain.

claim: Mice licking for gradations of sucrose showed a modest range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of sucrose elicited a greater number of licks.
source: Mice licking for gradations of sucrose (Figure 5C–I) showed a modest range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of sucrose elicited a greater number of licks (Figure 5F and H) and longer time spent licking during the trial (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the multi-spout sucrose experiments.

claim: Mice licking for gradations of quinine showed a modest range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of quinine elicited a lower number of licks.
source: Mice licking for gradations of quinine (Figure 5J–P, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) showed a modest range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of quinine elicited a lower number of licks (Loney and Meyer, 2018; Figure 5M and O) and shorter time spent licking during the trial (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the multi-spout quinine experiments and citation to prior work.

claim: Mice licking for gradations of NaCl showed a large range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of NaCl elicited a lower number of licks.
source: Mice licking for gradations of NaCl (Figure 5Q–W, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) showed a large range of licking behavior where trials with higher concentrations of NaCl elicited a lower number of licks (Figure 5T, V) and shorter time spent licking during the trial (Figure 5U).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the multi-spout NaCl experiments.

claim: Mice in the sucrose set started with high licking rates and showed a gradual satiation that resulted in decreased licking across all concentrations.
source: Mice in the sucrose set started with high licking rates and showed a gradual satiation that resulted in decreased licking across all concentrations (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D); mice in the quinine set started with high licking rates but rapidly dropped by around trial 40 across all concentrations (Figure 5P, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D); and mice in the NaCl set showed only a minor reduction in licking across all concentrations throughout the session (Figure 5W, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of licking behavior over the course of sessions.

claim: Mice displayed the highest number of licks during the sucrose set, then NaCl, then quinine.
source: Comparing the total number of licks per session across the three sets of solutions revealed that mice displayed the highest number of licks during the sucrose set, then NaCl, then quinine (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of total lick counts across solution sets.

claim: Mice in the quinine set showed substantially lower proportion of trials with licks compared to mice in the sets for sucrose or NaCl.
source: Comparing task engagement using the proportion of trials with licking across the three sets of solutions, mice in the quinine set showed substantially lower proportion of trials with licks compared to mice in the sets for sucrose or NaCl (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of trial engagement across solution sets.

claim: Older mice displayed higher lick rates for sucrose.
source: We also found that older mice displayed higher lick rates for sucrose (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K, L).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of age and licking behavior.

claim: There were no sex differences in task performance in the multi-spout assay, except a lower proportion of trials with licking in female mice.
source: Finally, we found no sex differences in task performance, except a lower proportion of trials with licking in female mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing male and female mice.

claim: Mice showed vastly different levels of total number of licks with the greatest number of licks for all concentrations under water restriction, then food restriction, then ad libitum.
source: Mice showed vastly different levels of total number of licks with the greatest number of licks for all concentrations under water restriction, then food restriction, then ad libitum (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing different homeostatic states.

claim: Mice displayed greater licking under the sodium-deplete state compared to the sodium-replete state.
source: Mice displayed greater licking under the sodium-deplete state compared to the sodium-replete state (Figure 6F–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–J).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing sodium demand states.

claim: Mice when sodium-deplete showed higher levels of licking for both water and 0.25 M NaCl.
source: Specifically, mice when sodium-deplete showed higher levels of licking for both water and 0.25 M NaCl.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from sodium demand experiments.

claim: The increased licking for water when sodium-deplete can potentially be attributed to higher levels of thirst, as previously described.
source: The increased licking for water when sodium-deplete can potentially be attributed to higher levels of thirst, as previously described (Jalowiec, 1974).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to prior work.

claim: During two sessions of free-access consumption, mice tested in the dark cycle consumed significantly more 10% sucrose compared to mice tested in the light cycle.
source: During two sessions of free-access consumption, mice tested in the dark cycle consumed significantly more 10% sucrose compared to mice tested in the light cycle (Figure 7B; Bainier et al., 2017; Smith, 2000; Tõnissaar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing light and dark cycle testing and citations to prior work.

claim: Experiments conducted during the light and dark cycle resulted in distinct licking across sucrose concentrations.
source: Despite similar overall licking in the multi-spout assay, we found that experiments conducted during the light and dark cycle resulted in distinct licking across sucrose concentrations (Figure 7E; Bainier et al., 2017; Tõnissaar et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing light and dark cycle testing and citations to prior work.

claim: Compared to mice tested in the light cycle, mice tested during the dark cycle showed higher levels of consumption early in the session.
source: Furthermore, compared to mice tested in the light cycle, mice tested during the dark cycle showed higher levels of consumption early in the session (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing light and dark cycle testing.

claim: There were no statistical differences in the mean licking for each concentration of sucrose across labs.
source: However, despite these nominal differences, there were no statistical differences in the mean licking for each concentration of sucrose across labs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing data from two independent labs.

claim: The activity of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons and the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens are well known to scale with relative reward value.
source: The activity of ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons and the release of dopamine in the nucleus accumbens are well known to scale with relative reward value such that the most rewarding stimuli produces increases in dopamine release and the least rewarding stimuli produces modest decreases in dopamine release (Eshel et al., 2015; Hajnal et al., 2004; Tobler et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During consumption of sucrose under food restriction, strong scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in the NAcShL and moderate scaling in the NAcShM was measured.
source: During consumption of sucrose under food restriction, where we observe a large range in licking across concentrations of sucrose (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, left), we measured strong scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in the NAcShL and moderate scaling in the NAcShM (representative mouse [Figure 8D]; mean fluorescence [Figure 8E]; mean fluorescence during access [Figure 8F]; cumulative distribution function [CDF] shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data during the multi-spout task.

claim: Significantly higher GRAB-DA responses in the NAcShL compared to the NAcShM were observed at higher concentrations of sucrose under food restriction.
source: Specifically, we observed significantly higher responses in the NAcShL compared to the NAcShM at higher concentrations of sucrose (10%, 20%, and 30%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of fiber photometry data.

claim: On a trial-by-trial basis, a correlation between the amount of licking on a trial and GRAB-DA fluorescence was observed during sucrose consumption under food restriction.
source: On a trial-by-trial basis, we observed a correlation between the amount of licking on a trial and GRAB-DA fluorescence (Figure 8G; CDF shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of fiber photometry and behavioral data.

claim: During consumption of sucrose under water restriction, moderate scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in the NAcShL and little scaling in the NAcShM was measured.
source: During consumption of sucrose under water restriction, where we observe high levels of licking but minimal range of licking across concentrations of sucrose (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, mid), we measured moderate scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in the NAcShL and little scaling in the NAcShM (representative mouse [Figure 8H]; mean fluorescence [Figure 8I]; mean fluorescence during access [Figure 8J]; CDF shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data during the multi-spout task.

claim: During consumption of NaCl under water restriction, strong scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in both the NAcShL and NAcShM was measured.
source: During consumption of the aversive tastant (NaCl) under water restriction, where we observed a large range of licking across concentrations of NaCl (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, right), we measured strong scaling of GRAB-DA fluorescence in both the NAcShL and NAcShM (representative mouse [Figure 8L], mean fluorescence [Figure 8M]; mean fluorescence during access [Figure 8N]; CDF shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by fiber photometry data during the multi-spout task.

claim: A strong correlation in GRAB-DA fluorescence in the NAcShL and NAcShM was found across each stage of the task.
source: Taking advantage of the head-fixed preparation, we were able to record the activity of the NAcShL and NAcShM simultaneously and found a strong correlation in GRAB-DA fluorescence in the two regions across each stage of the task (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of simultaneous fiber photometry recordings.

claim: The NAcShM shows a disproportionately higher range of GRAB-DA fluorescence during multi-spout consumption of NaCl compared to the other stages of the task.
source: The NAcShM shows a disproportionately higher range of GRAB-DA fluorescence during multi-spout consumption of NaCl compared to the other stages of the task (Figure 8—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the range of dopamine signals across different task stages.

claim: The higher range of dopamine release in the NAcShM during consumption of a range of aversive solutions compared to appetitive solutions could indicate a specialized role for the NAcShM in mediating behavioral responses to aversive stimuli.
source: The higher range of dopamine release in the NAcShM during consumption of a range of aversive solutions compared to appetitive solutions could indicate a specialized role for the NAcShM in mediating behavioral responses to aversive stimuli as previously described for footshock conditioning (de Jong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Head fixation can be acutely stressful to mice and causes increased levels of circulating stress markers.
